Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FortiGate SSL VPN authentication brute-force burst (FortiBleed harvesting campaign) · [LLM] Microsoft SQL Server brute-force burst correlated with FortiBleed operator MO
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FortiGate SSL VPN successful login from anonymizer/new-geography post-FortiBleed · [LLM] FortiGate management/admin portal login success from public internet source
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
FortiGate SSL VPN successful login from anonymizer/new-geography post-FortiBleed AIExploitation High
Hunts for successful FortiGate SSL VPN authentications from IPs/countries the user has never authenticated from before — the expected access pattern after the FortiBleed dataset of 73,932 firewall URLs with plaintext credentials gets weaponised. Article-specific because affected orgs are named (Chevron, Samsung, Foxconn, Comcast, AT&T, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Sinopec, State Grid) and Beaumont confirmed the creds are live. Rationale: The article + Beaumont/Hudson Rock corroboration confirms 73,932 FortiGate URLs with plaintext SSL VPN credentials are live. Detecting a successful SSL VPN auth from an IP the user has never used before is the cleanest indicator of leaked-cred reuse. The CommonSecurityLog connector is Microsoft's recommended Fortinet path (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall). Cross-checked against: • https://www.kevinbeaumont.com/ • https://www.hudsonrock.com/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall
ATT&CKT1078 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Network_Sessions.All_Sessions
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user traveling and connecting from hotel/airport Wi-Fi for the first time
  • Mobile workers with carrier-grade NAT IPs that rotate weekly
  • Newly hired employee's first VPN connection
  • Vendor / contractor connecting from their own corporate IP for the first time
  • Disaster-recovery / failover routing the VPN client to a different egress
Suppression filter
| where SrcCountry !in ("<list-of-employee-travel-countries>") or DestinationUserName !in (dynamic(["<known-mobile-workers>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DestinationUserName + SourceIP, geo-locate, confirm with the user via out-of-band channel that they initiated the session. Check baseline ASN/country vs the new one. 2) Contain: if unconfirmed, force-disconnect the SSL VPN session on the FortiGate (`diag sys session clear`), invalidate the user's password, revoke active tokens, and require MFA re-enrollment. Block the source IP at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SourceIP across all FortiGate, AAD, and ImAuthentication tables for 30 days; pivot on DestinationUserName for any internal lateral-movement signals (RDP / SMB / Kerberos TGS), and check whether the user appears in the Hudson Rock FortiBleed lookup.
// FortiGate SSL VPN logs typically arrive via 3rd-party MDE connector or surface in DeviceLogonEvents only when the VPN client logs onto the endpoint. Best-effort: surface RemoteInteractive/Network logons immediately preceded by VPN client connect, from non-corp IPs.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let KnownCorpSubnets = dynamic(["10.","172.16.","172.17.","172.18.","172.19.","172.20.","172.21.","172.22.","172.23.","172.24.","172.25.","172.26.","172.27.","172.28.","172.29.","172.30.","172.31.","192.168."]);
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where LogonType in ("RemoteInteractive","Network")
| where isnotempty(RemoteIP) and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not(RemoteIP startswith_cs KnownCorpSubnets[0])
| join kind=leftanti (
    DeviceLogonEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(60d) .. ago(LookbackDays))
    | where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
    | summarize by AccountName, RemoteIP
) on AccountName, RemoteIP
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain, LogonType, RemoteIP, RemoteDeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// FortiGate sends CEF/syslog to CommonSecurityLog (Fortinet AzMonitor connector)
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let BaselineDays = 60d;
let Baseline =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(LookbackDays))
    | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
    | where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
    | where Activity has_any ("ssl vpn login","sslvpn-login","sslvpn_session_user_login_event")
    | where DeviceAction =~ "login" or Message has "login successfully"
    | summarize by DestinationHostName, SourceIP;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
| where Activity has_any ("ssl vpn login","sslvpn-login","sslvpn_session_user_login_event")
| where DeviceAction =~ "login" or Message has "login successfully"
| where isnotempty(DestinationHostName) and isnotempty(SourceIP)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DestinationHostName, SourceIP
| extend GeoIP = geo_info_from_ip_address(SourceIP)
| extend SrcCountry = tostring(GeoIP.country)
| project TimeGenerated, User=DestinationHostName, SourceIP, SrcCountry, DeviceName=DestinationHostName, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fortinet SSL VPN Successful Login From New Source IP (FortiBleed)
id: 7a3b2c4e-9d1f-4b18-8f63-1a5b9d2e3c44
status: experimental
description: Detects successful FortiGate SSL VPN authentication from a source IP not previously observed for that user — high-fidelity post-FortiBleed credential-use indicator.

FortiGate SSL VPN authentication brute-force burst (FortiBleed harvesting campaign) AIDelivery High
Detects high-volume failed SSL VPN authentication attempts against FortiGate from a single source IP — the exact behavior Diachenko reported (1.16 billion credential attempts against 320,777 FortiGate targets). Threshold-based count over a 10-minute window per source IP, matching the operator-scale brute-force campaign harvesting these credentials. Rationale: Diachenko's investigation enumerated 1.16B credential attempts across 320,777 FortiGate targets — a brute-force pattern that produces a clear high-volume failed-auth burst signature in FortiGate event logs. 50 failures/10min from one IP is well above legitimate fat-finger behavior. CommonSecurityLog DestinationUserName/SourceIP are the canonical CEF fields. Cross-checked against: • https://www.hudsonrock.com/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1110.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured FortiClient on a laptop with stale cached credentials looping
  • Penetration testing engagement against the FortiGate
  • RADIUS / LDAP backend outage causing valid auth to register as failure
  • Stale service account in a script repeatedly attempting connection
  • Vulnerability scanner enumerating SSL VPN response codes
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<known-pentest-ips>","<vuln-scanner-ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is external; check SampleUsers for password-spray pattern (many users) vs single-user brute-force; geo-IP the source. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the perimeter and FortiGate's quarantine list, enable lockout policy if not active, force password rotation on any accounts that subsequently authenticated successfully from that IP. 3) Hunt: pivot the SourceIP across 30 days for any successful login from the same source; cross-check the impacted FortiGate's external URL against the Hudson Rock FortiBleed lookup tool to determine prior exposure.
// FortiGate brute-force telemetry is not natively in MDE. Best-effort proxy: outbound public IPs touching VPN endpoints from EDR perspective is not the right surface. Use sentinel_kql instead.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 443
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("FortiClient.exe","FortiSSLVPNdaemon.exe")
| summarize Attempts=count() by RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where Attempts > 30
| order by Timestamp desc
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let AttemptThreshold = 50;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
| where Activity has_any ("ssl vpn login fail","sslvpn-login-fail","ssl_vpn_login_fail")
   or Message has_any ("ssl_login_fail","sslvpn_login_fail","login failed")
| summarize Attempts=count(),
            UniqueUsers=dcount(DestinationHostName),
            SampleUsers=make_set(DestinationHostName, 10)
            by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where Attempts >= AttemptThreshold
| extend GeoIP = geo_info_from_ip_address(SourceIP), SrcCountry = tostring(GeoIP.country)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:fortinet @evt.name:(*sslvpn* OR *ssl_vpn*) @evt.outcome:failure
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="fortigate" Authentication.action="failure" (Authentication.signature="ssl-login-fail" OR Authentication.signature="sslvpn_login_fail") by Authentication.src_ip _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where count >= 50 | iplocation src_ip | table _time src_ip count Country City
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="fortigate" Authentication.action="failure" (Authentication.signature="ssl-login-fail" OR Authentication.signature="sslvpn_login_fail") by Authentication.src_ip _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where count >= 50 | iplocation src_ip | table _time src_ip count Country City
Microsoft SQL Server brute-force burst correlated with FortiBleed operator MO AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for high-volume failed SQL Server authentication attempts (event 18456) against internet-exposed MSSQL — Diachenko reported the same operators conducted 2.1 billion credential attempts against 163,650 MSSQL targets alongside the FortiGate campaign. Detection is specific because it threshold-correlates failed SQL logon counts the way the operators ran them in parallel with the FortiGate campaign. Rationale: Article explicitly quantifies 2.1B SQL Server credential attempts against 163,650 MSSQL hosts conducted by the same operators. EventID 18456 is the canonical SQL auth-failure ID and the SecurityEvent / SQL ERRORLOG fields are well-defined. Threshold of 100/10min cleanly separates this from app-tier connection-pool churn. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/errors-events/mssqlserver-18456-database-engine-error • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fortibleed-leak-exposes-fortinet-vpn-credentials-for-73-000-devices/
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1110.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • App tier with rotated credentials looping reconnection attempts
  • Sysadmin running sqlcmd with wrong password while troubleshooting
  • DBA toolset (DBeaver/SSMS) connecting to retired instance with old creds
  • Vulnerability scanner enumerating MSSQL versions
  • Failover cluster transient auth churn during AG failover
Suppression filter
| where IpAddress !in (dynamic(["<app-tier-subnets>"])) and Computer !startswith "AG-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check IpAddress source — internal app servers warrant a credential-rotation conversation, external IPs warrant block-first; review SampleAccounts for sa/admin enumeration. 2) Contain: block external SourceIP at perimeter, disable SQL Server Authentication on internet-exposed instances if not required, force `sa` password rotation, enable account lockout. 3) Hunt: pivot the IpAddress across 30 days for successful SQL auth, check for follow-on xp_cmdshell, SQLCLR, or BCP/openrowset abuse, and confirm whether the SQL host is also a FortiGate-protected segment listed in the FortiBleed dataset.
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sqlservr.exe"
| summarize Attempts=count(),
            UniqueAccounts=dcount(AccountName),
            SampleAccounts=make_set(AccountName, 10)
            by DeviceName, RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, WindowMinutes)
| where Attempts >= 100
| order by Timestamp desc
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 18456
   or (EventID == 4625 and ProcessName has "sqlservr.exe")
| summarize Attempts=count(),
            UniqueAccounts=dcount(TargetUserName),
            SampleAccounts=make_set(TargetUserName, 10)
            by Computer, IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where Attempts >= 100
| extend GeoIP = geo_info_from_ip_address(IpAddress), SrcCountry = tostring(GeoIP.country)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.security @EventID:18456
#event_simpleName=UserLogon LogonStatus!=0 
| ImageFileName=/sqlservr\.exe/i 
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=[count()]) 
| _count >= 100
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="mssql" Authentication.action="failure" by Authentication.src_ip Authentication.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | stats sum(count) as Attempts dc(user) as UniqUsers values(user) as Users by src_ip | where Attempts >= 100
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="mssql" Authentication.action="failure" by Authentication.src_ip Authentication.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | stats sum(count) as Attempts dc(user) as UniqUsers values(user) as Users by src_ip | where Attempts >= 100
FortiGate management/admin portal login success from public internet source AIExploitation Medium
Detects successful FortiGate administrative GUI / SSH / API authentication where the source IP is on the public internet — the exact exposure Beaumont called out ("a majority of the affected devices expose their FortiGate management interfaces directly to the internet"). Pairs the leaked admin credentials in the FortiBleed dataset with the misconfiguration that lets them be used remotely. Rationale: Beaumont's analysis (cited in the article) confirms that a majority of the 73k+ affected FortiGate devices have management interfaces exposed to the public internet, and the FortiBleed dataset contains admin credentials extracted from FortiGate configs. Successful admin authentication from a non-RFC1918 source is a high-fidelity indicator that a leaked credential is being used. CommonSecurityLog columns used (DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, DeviceAction, SourceIP, DestinationUserName, DestinationHostName, Message) are all canonical CEF fields for the Fortinet connector. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kevinbeaumont.com/ • https://www.hudsonrock.com/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall
ATT&CKT1078 T1133 T1556
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network engineer working from home over residential ISP without site-to-site VPN
  • MSP / Fortinet partner managing the firewall from their own corporate IP
  • Fortinet TAC / professional services session over public Internet
  • Out-of-band administrative session during a site-to-site VPN outage
  • Cloud-hosted FortiGate (Azure / AWS) where mgmt interface is intentionally public and ACL'd
Suppression filter
| where AdminUser !in (dynamic(["<MSP-admin-name>","fortinet-tac"])) and SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<MSP-egress-ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull SourceIP, geo-locate, and confirm via change-management whether the engineer scheduled an out-of-band admin session; review the FortiGate's `config system admin` trusthost ACL to see whether the source was allow-listed. 2) Contain: if unconfirmed, force-disconnect the admin session, rotate every admin credential on the device (`config system admin` + `set password`), restrict mgmt-interface access to trusthost CIDRs only, and enable MFA on admin accounts. 3) Hunt: pivot SourceIP across all FortiGate logs for 30 days for config-change events (`config system`, `config firewall policy`); check the FortiGate's configuration for unauthorized backdoor admin accounts or VPN portals; verify the device's external URL against Hudson Rock's FortiBleed lookup tool.
// FortiGate admin-portal auth does not surface on Defender XDR; CommonSecurityLog (Sentinel) is the right pivot. Best-effort EDR proxy: outbound HTTPS/SSH from admin workstations to FortiGate management IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (22, 443, 8443)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("putty.exe","plink.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
| where Activity has_any ("admin login","admin_login_success","login","login successful")
   or Message has_any ("User admin login successfully","login succeeded from","Administrator","logged in successfully")
| where isnotempty(SourceIP)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| extend GeoIP = geo_info_from_ip_address(SourceIP), SrcCountry = tostring(GeoIP.country)
| project TimeGenerated,
          AdminUser = coalesce(DestinationHostName, SourceUserName),
          FortiGate = DestinationHostName,
          SourceIP,
          SrcCountry,
          Activity,
          DeviceAction,
          Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JetBrains IDE plaintext HTTP egress to public IP (LLMjacking exfil pattern) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host beaconing to the attacker-controlled C2 IP 39.107.60.51 named in the Aikido write-up. The malicious JetBrains plugins POST the entered OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API key in cleartext HTTP to this address. Rationale: Single hard-coded C2 IP (39.107.60.51) from the article body — Aikido confirms it's where every one of the 15 plugins POSTs the stolen key in plaintext HTTP. Any internal host talking to that IP is a confirmed compromise.
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox/range explicitly testing the IOC
  • Security researcher repro of the Aikido write-up on a managed workstation
  • Honeypot / canary host instrumented to call the C2 deliberately
  • Geo-IP scanners sweeping the /24 (will hit port-scan signature, not the post-payload pattern)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","smartscreen.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the parent process + command line of the connecting process on the affected device — if it is idea64.exe / pycharm64.exe / any JetBrains IDE binary, assume LLMjacking and treat any OpenAI/DeepSeek/Anthropic key that user touched in the last 60 days as burned. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the device via MDE Live Response, force-rotate every AI provider API key in the user's vault, revoke OAuth tokens to the same providers, and block 39.107.60.51 at egress. 3) HUNT: pivot on the InstalledPlugins manifest under %APPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins for any of the 15 package IDs (org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.json.simple.kit, etc.) across the fleet; query AI provider billing for spikes coinciding with the install date.
let JetBrainsProcs = dynamic(["idea64.exe","idea.exe","pycharm64.exe","webstorm64.exe","phpstorm64.exe","clion64.exe","rider64.exe","goland64.exe","datagrip64.exe","rustrover64.exe","rubymine64.exe","appcode.exe","studio64.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51"
| extend IsJetBrainsHost = InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (JetBrainsProcs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, IsJetBrainsHost
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, NetworkBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin package-ID dropped under user plugins dir AIDelivery High
Detects file creation events for any of the 15 Aikido-attributed malicious JetBrains plugin package IDs (org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.json.simple.kit, etc.) inside the per-user plugin directory. Fires at install time on every JetBrains IDE. Rationale: Article enumerates all 15 attacker-attributed plugin package IDs verbatim plus the standard JetBrains per-user plugin layout. File-event match on the package ID under any *\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins\* path is unambiguous.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating samples from the Aikido write-up in an isolated VM
  • MDR detonation lab pulling the plugin from the JetBrains Marketplace for analysis
  • Tabletop / purple-team exercise
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mssense.exe","msmpeng.exe","smartscreen.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm the developer actually installed the plugin (not a sample pulled by AV/IR tooling) by checking InitiatingProcessFileName — should be the JetBrains IDE binary itself or its updater, not an analyst tool. 2) CONTAIN: remove the plugin directory, revoke and rotate every AI provider API key the developer has ever pasted into a JetBrains IDE settings panel (OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, SiliconFlow), and block 39.107.60.51 at egress as a belt-and-braces step. 3) HUNT: query AI provider audit logs for unfamiliar IP ranges using the developer's keys in the 24h after install; expand search for any of the 15 package IDs across all developer workstations.

Malicious Chrome ad-blocker extension installed (Smart Adblocker / Adblock for Browser) AIInstallation High
Detects the presence of either Smart Adblocker (iojpcjjdfhlcbgjnpngcmaojmlokmeii) or Adblock for Browser (jcbjcocinigpbgfpnhlpagidbmlngnnn) extension directories on managed endpoints. Both extensions are confirmed by PromptSnatcher researcher to exfiltrate AI chatbot conversation history. Rationale: Two exact Chrome Web Store extension IDs from the article (iojpcjjdfhlcbgjnpngcmaojmlokmeii and jcbjcocinigpbgfpnhlpagidbmlngnnn) plus standard Chrome per-user extension directory layout. Extension IDs are immutable in the Chrome Web Store, so the match is unambiguous and persists across the extension's auto-updates.
ATT&CKT1176 T1119
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher reproducing the PromptSnatcher article in a VM
  • EDR / sandbox auto-installing the extension as part of malware analysis
  • Help-desk image with the extension preinstalled before the disclosure (legacy artefact, no active intent)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the logged-on user and inventory which AI chatbot accounts (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Grok, Meta AI) the user has used in Chrome — assume every conversation since the extension install date is compromised. 2) CONTAIN: remove the extension directory, sign the user out of all AI chatbot sessions, rotate any credentials or secrets pasted into chat prompts. 3) HUNT: pivot the extension ID across all managed Chrome installs, check for the same exfiltration pattern (chrome.exe parent making POST requests to non-public-filter-list domains) on those hosts.
let BadExtIds = dynamic(["iojpcjjdfhlcbgjnpngcmaojmlokmeii","jcbjcocinigpbgfpnhlpagidbmlngnnn"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\Chrome\\User Data\\","/Chrome/Default/Extensions/","/google-chrome/Default/Extensions/","/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Extensions/")
| where FolderPath has_any (BadExtIds)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
let BadExtIds = dynamic(["iojpcjjdfhlcbgjnpngcmaojmlokmeii","jcbjcocinigpbgfpnhlpagidbmlngnnn"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\Chrome\\User Data\\","/Chrome/Default/Extensions/","/google-chrome/Default/Extensions/")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (BadExtIds)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath
| order by LastSeen desc

JetBrains IDE process initiates plaintext HTTP POST to external IP AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for any JetBrains IDE binary making an outbound TCP/80 (plaintext HTTP) connection to a public IP — which is the exact exfil shape Aikido describes ("over an HTTP request in plaintext format"). Legitimate JetBrains telemetry and plugin update channels are HTTPS. Rationale: Aikido explicitly calls out the plaintext-HTTP exfil shape ("siphon the provided API key to a remote server over an HTTP request in plaintext format"). JetBrains IDEs normally talk HTTPS for everything — any TCP/80 from idea64.exe et al. to a public IP is anomalous. Catches future variants that change the C2 IP off 39.107.60.51.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Plugin update server briefly redirecting via HTTP before HTTPS upgrade
  • Captive-portal detection probe from the IDE on first-launch in a hotel/coffee-shop network
  • Corporate web proxy doing HTTP CONNECT termination then proxying to upstream HTTPS
  • Internal development plugin repositories served over plain HTTP on a private DNS-resolved hostname
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".jetbrains.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".intellij.net" and RemoteUrl !endswith "plugins.jetbrains.com"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: capture full URL and body size of the HTTP POST — if the URL path contains 'key', 'token', 'auth', or the request size is small (<2KB) the LLMjacking pattern is highly likely. Cross-check the destination IP against threat intel for known JetBrains plugin C2 (39.107.60.51 confirmed). 2) CONTAIN: block the destination IP at egress and isolate the device pending plugin inventory. 3) HUNT: enumerate installed plugins via %APPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins on the device, check each plugin's vendor.xml against the 15 IDs from the Aikido write-up, then sweep the fleet for any plugin sharing the same vendor URL or signing cert.

JetBrains plugin manifest dropped under user-writable plugins directory by non-IDE process AIInstallation Medium
Persistence pivot: catches a plugin.xml or META-INF\plugin.xml being written under a per-user JetBrains plugins directory by a process that ISN'T the JetBrains IDE installer itself — useful for catching out-of-band installs (manual disk drops, packaging scripts, malware) that bypass Marketplace flow but still load on next IDE start. Rationale: Catches lateral-movement / sideloading variants of the Aikido campaign — even if the attacker pivots off the Marketplace, the plugin still has to land plugin.xml inside the per-user JetBrains plugins folder to be auto-loaded by the IDE. Excluding the IDE's own binaries narrows to out-of-band writes (script, archive extractor, malware dropper).
ATT&CKT1547.014 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually unzipping a plugin from a downloaded .zip (7zip.exe / explorer.exe as ActingProcess)
  • DevOps tooling provisioning plugins via Ansible/Chef/Puppet (likely an agent process)
  • Backup software restoring the plugins directory
  • Custom enterprise plugin distribution scripts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","installer.exe","chef-client.exe","puppet.exe","ansible.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: read the dropped plugin.xml — look for the <id> tag and cross-check against the 15 known-malicious IDs (org.sm.yms.toolkit etc.) and any vendor URL that resolves to a non-JetBrains domain. 2) CONTAIN: delete the plugin directory before next IDE start (else it auto-loads) and capture a copy for analysis. 3) HUNT: pivot on ActingProcessName to see what else that process touched on the host; query EDR for the same process writing plugin.xml on any other developer workstation.
let JetBrainsProcs = dynamic(["idea64.exe","idea.exe","pycharm64.exe","webstorm64.exe","phpstorm64.exe","clion64.exe","rider64.exe","goland64.exe","datagrip64.exe","rustrover64.exe","rubymine64.exe","toolbox.exe","appcode.exe","studio64.exe"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "plugin.xml"
| where FolderPath has "JetBrains" and FolderPath has "plugins"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (JetBrainsProcs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let JetBrainsProcs = dynamic(["idea64.exe","idea.exe","pycharm64.exe","webstorm64.exe","phpstorm64.exe","clion64.exe","rider64.exe","goland64.exe","datagrip64.exe","rustrover64.exe","rubymine64.exe","toolbox.exe"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "plugin.xml"
| where TargetFilePath has "JetBrains" and TargetFilePath has "plugins"
| where ActingProcessName !in~ (JetBrainsProcs)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:*\\JetBrains\\*\\plugins\\*\\plugin.xml -@Image:(*\\idea64.exe OR *\\idea.exe OR *\\pycharm64.exe OR *\\webstorm64.exe OR *\\phpstorm64.exe OR *\\clion64.exe OR *\\rider64.exe OR *\\goland64.exe OR *\\datagrip64.exe OR *\\rustrover64.exe OR *\\rubymine64.exe OR *\\toolbox.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| regex("(?i)\\\\JetBrains\\\\.+\\\\plugins\\\\.+\\\\plugin\\.xml$", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(idea64|idea|pycharm64|webstorm64|phpstorm64|clion64|rider64|goland64|datagrip64|rustrover64|rubymine64|toolbox)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:

level: high

status: experimental
description: |

references:

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard

| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Joomla JCE profile.import unauthenticated RCE attempt (CVE-2026-48907) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to the Joomla JCE plugin's profile-creation/import endpoint by unauthenticated clients — the exploitation primitive for CVE-2026-48907 that lets attackers register a rogue editor profile and upload a PHP webshell. Surfaces both successful (HTTP 200/302) and probing attempts against IIS-fronted or WAF-protected Joomla installs. Rationale: Article identifies the exact Joomla JCE plugin and the precise exploitation primitive ("creation of new editor profiles for unauthenticated users" → "upload and execution of PHP code"). The detection pivots on the JCE-specific URL components (com_jce, task=plugin, imgmanager, filemanager) which are unique strings appearing only in this plugin's HTTP request shape. Cross-checked CISA KEV and JCE vendor advisory referenced in body. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48907 • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://www.joomlacontenteditor.net/news/security
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated Joomla administrators legitimately using the JCE WYSIWYG editor's filemanager
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Nuclei templates for CVE-2026-48907) probing the endpoint
  • Internal pentest engagements explicitly testing this CVE
  • Web crawlers (Googlebot, Bingbot) following old JCE URLs from search index
  • Site backup/migration tools that GET admin URLs to verify content
Suppression filter
| where not (cIP in ("<authenticated_admin_ip_pool>")) and csUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","Googlebot","bingbot")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Pull the full HTTP request body and the immediately following requests from the same SourceIP — look for POST to a newly-created profile path, then a GET to a PHP file under /images/, /tmp/, or /media/ (the JCE upload landing zones). Identify the rogue profile name in the Joomla #__jce_profiles DB table. Step 2 (Contain): Block the SourceIP at the edge / WAF. Take the Joomla site offline or put into maintenance mode if compromise is confirmed. Reset all admin passwords, DB credentials, and hosting account credentials per the JCE vendor guidance — patching alone does not evict the attacker. Step 3 (Hunt): Pivot to DeviceFileEvents for new .php/.phtml files written by w3wp/httpd/php-fpm under web-root in the last 30d; pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for php-cgi or w3wp spawning cmd.exe/powershell.exe/bash; check egress to the article's published IPs (107.149.130.5, 92.38.150.143, 45.153.129.241).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where LocalPort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","apache2","nginx","php-fpm")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("com_jce","index.php?option=com_jce","task=plugin","imgmanager","filemanager")
   or AdditionalFields has_any ("com_jce","profile.import")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Pivot 1: IIS W3C logs (Computer is the host column, NOT DeviceName)
let IISHits = W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "com_jce" or csUriQuery has_any ("com_jce","task=plugin","profile","imgmanager","filemanager")
| where scStatus < 400 or scStatus == 200
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Host=sSiteName, ClientIP=cIP, Method=csMethod, Uri=csUriStem, Query=csUriQuery, Status=scStatus, UA=csUserAgent;
// Pivot 2: WAF / proxy CEF (use DestinationHostName / RequestURL, NOT DeviceName)
let WAFHits = CommonSecurityLog

Inbound HTTP from published CVE-2026-48907 JCE exploitation IPs AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces any inbound web traffic from the three IPs publicly reported as participating in automated mass exploitation of the Joomla JCE flaw. Because the campaign is automated and indiscriminate, an inbound connection from any of these IPs to a Joomla-hosting web server is high-fidelity even without a request-body match. Rationale: Article pre-extracted three IPs (107.149.130.5, 92.38.150.143, 45.153.129.241) associated with CVE-2026-48907 mass exploitation. Because the article itself states attacks are automated and indiscriminate ("a site with no public registration is not safe"), any inbound TCP/80/443 from these IPs to a Joomla-hosting server is a strong campaign indicator independent of URL match. Note: the W3CIISLog/CommonSecurityLog/ImNetworkSession schemas use Computer/DestinationHostName/DvcHostname respectively rather than DeviceName; the CloudWatch query targets the VPC flow log group (not CloudTrail) because that is where srcAddr/dstAddr fields naturally live. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IP reassignment if the abuse-hosting provider reclaims the IP and re-leases it to a benign tenant (decays over time, validate weekly)
  • Threat-intel researchers / honeypot operators legitimately scanning from these same IPs
  • Defensive scanners that purposely route through these IPs to test detections
  • Tor exit nodes (none of the three are currently listed, but possible reassignment)
Suppression filter
| where not (DvcHostname has_any ("honeypot","canary","decoy-"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Confirm the targeted host runs Joomla and check whether the JCE plugin is installed and on a vulnerable version (pre-2.9.99.6). Examine W3CIISLog/CommonSecurityLog for the immediately-following request from the same source — a POST creating an editor profile or a GET fetching a PHP file under /images, /tmp, or /media. Step 2 (Contain): Drop the three IPs at the perimeter firewall and WAF. If a successful exploitation request is observed (HTTP 200 to a profile-creation URL), isolate the web host pending forensic triage. Step 3 (Hunt): Search 90 days backwards for any prior connections from these IPs to your Joomla estate. Hunt for new PHP files under web-root written by the web-server process and outbound connections from the web host to suspicious destinations (reverse-shell callbacks). Reset Joomla admin, DB, and hosting passwords if compromise is confirmed — per vendor guidance the patch does not evict an already-present attacker.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionFound")
| where RemoteIP in ("107.149.130.5","92.38.150.143","45.153.129.241")
| where LocalPort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
// Pivot 1: IIS W3C logs (Computer is the host column)
let IISFromBadIP = W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where cIP in ("107.149.130.5","92.38.150.143","45.153.129.241")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP=cIP, Method=csMethod, Uri=csUriStem, Query=csUriQuery, Status=scStatus, UA=csUserAgent;
// Pivot 2: Firewall / WAF (use SourceIP / DestinationHostName — DeviceName is NOT on this table)
let CEFFromBadIP = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SourceIP in ("107.149.130.5","92.38.150.143","45.153.129.241")
| project TimeGenerated, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, ClientIP=SourceIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct;
// Pivot 3: ASIM network sessions (DvcHostname is the host column on ImNetworkSession)
let ASIMFromBadIP = ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SrcIpAddr in ("107.149.130.5","92.38.150.143","45.153.129.241")
| where DstPortNumber in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, DvcAction;
union IISFromBadIP, CEFFromBadIP, ASIMFromBadIP
| order by TimeGenerated desc

High

144 Mastra npm Packages Compromised via Hijacked Contributor Account

The Hacker NewsAikidoStepSecurity
2026-06-17 11 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On June 17, 2026, an attacker compromised the @mastra npm organization and quietly added easy-day-js as a dependency across 140+ packages in the Mastra AI framework ecosystem. easy-day-js is a typosquat of the popular dayjs date library, and its latest version contained an obfuscated postinstall dropper that downloaded and ran a second-stage payload from attacker-controlled servers, then deleted itself to remove any trace. Packages with a combined weekly download count exceeding 1.1 million were exposed. If you installed any @mastra package today, treat your environment as compromised.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm install referencing compromised @mastra packages or easy-day-js dependency
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — 144 Mastra npm Packages Compromised via Hijacked Contributor Account
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] easy-day-js postinstall hook running node setup.cjs --no-warnings · [LLM] Node spawning detached script from %TEMP% with 24-hex filename and host:port argv (stage-2) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound HTTPS to Mastra supply-chain C2 23.254.164.92:8000 and 23.254.164.123:443 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Mastra dropper beacon file .pkg_history/.pkg_logs created by node in temp directory · [LLM] node.exe reading developer credential files shortly after npm install (Mastra stage-2)
easy-day-js postinstall hook running node setup.cjs --no-warnings AIInstallation High
Detects the @mastra supply-chain dropper's entry point: a node.exe process executing setup.cjs with the warning-suppression flag, almost always spawned from an npm/npx/yarn parent during package install. The string pair is unique to this campaign. Rationale: The literal cmdline pair 'setup.cjs' + '--no-warnings' is the postinstall hook defined in the malicious easy-day-js@1.11.22 package.json verbatim from the article. Combined with an npm/npx/yarn parent it has no legitimate analog in production environments. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra/issues/18045 • https://app.stepsecurity.io/oss-security-feed/@mastra/schema-compat?version=1.2.12
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546.016 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer-written test fixture literally named setup.cjs in an internal package's postinstall
  • Internal Node.js tooling that happens to chain --no-warnings into a build script called setup.cjs
  • Security research labs detonating the IOC sample for analysis
  • Vendored npm modules where a maintainer reused the filename setup.cjs for legitimate bootstrap
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jest","mocha","vitest","--test") and ProcessCommandLine !contains "easy-day-js")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the host's npm/yarn lockfile and confirm if easy-day-js@1.11.22 or any @mastra package version listed in the article is resolved. Capture SHA256 of the setup.cjs file and compare against IOCs 221c45a7…, 4a886024…, ae70dd4f…. 2) Contain: isolate the host (developer workstation or CI runner), revoke any NPM_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY/OPENAI_API_KEY/AWS keys present on the box, kill any node child process still running, force-rotate org-level npm publish tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessAccountName + DeviceId to find any node child writing to %TEMP%\<24-hex>.js, any connection to 23.254.164.0/24, and any reads of ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.npmrc, or .github/workflows secrets directories in the 60 minutes following the postinstall.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.cjs" and ProcessCommandLine has "--no-warnings"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","npm-cli.js","npx.exe","npx","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","cmd.exe","bash","sh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256

SecurityEvent

Outbound HTTPS to Mastra supply-chain C2 23.254.164.92:8000 and 23.254.164.123:443 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host (dev workstation or CI runner) connecting to the stage-1 download server 23.254.164.92:8000 or stage-2 exfil server 23.254.164.123:443, including their hostwinds DNS aliases. These IPs and the /update/<numeric-id> URI shape are unique to this campaign. Rationale: Both /24-adjacent IPs and both hostwinds aliases are explicit IOCs in the article body and kill-chain reconstruction. The /update/49890878 URI path is the literal stage-1 endpoint copied verbatim from the article. Any hit is a high-fidelity infection indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra/issues/18045 • https://app.stepsecurity.io/oss-security-feed/@mastra/schema-compat?version=1.2.12
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001 T1571 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat intelligence analysts manually visiting the C2 from a sandbox
  • Internal blue-team red-team exercises replaying the IOC list
  • Internet-wide scanners (Censys, Shodan, Project Discovery) operating from corporate egress
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("WindowsSandboxClient.exe","sandbox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessFileName for the connection — if it's node.exe with a parent of npm/npx/yarn, treat as confirmed Mastra supply-chain infection. Capture the full lockfile and resolved easy-day-js / @mastra package versions. 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.0/24 and both hwsrv-1327785/6.hostwindsdns.com at perimeter and proxy, isolate any host that connected, kill all node child processes. 3) Hunt: rotate every secret accessible from that host: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, AWS keys, GITHUB_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN. Search SigninLogs / CloudTrail / GitHub audit log for any use of those tokens from non-corporate IPs in the 24h window starting at the first connection.
let badIPs = dynamic(["23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123"]);
let badDomains = dynamic(["hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com","hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (badIPs)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (badDomains)
   or RemoteUrl has "/update/49890878"
| extend Stage = case(RemoteIP == "23.254.164.92" or RemoteUrl has "hwsrv-1327786", "Stage1-Download",
                     RemoteIP == "23.254.164.123" or RemoteUrl has "hwsrv-1327785", "Stage2-Exfil", "Unknown")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Stage, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let badIPs = dynamic(["23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123"]);
let badDomains = dynamic(["hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com","hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationIP in (badIPs) or DestinationHostName in (badDomains) or RequestURL has "/update/49890878"
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceVendor),
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name in (badDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses=RemoteIp),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr in (badIPs) or DstHostname in (badDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mastra Supply-Chain C2 Network Connection (23.254.164.92 / 23.254.164.123)
id: 9c8f1d2e-4b3a-44e1-9d52-c6f9c7e2a83a
description: Detects outbound connection to the @mastra npm supply-chain attack C2 infrastructure used by easy-day-js@1.11.22 dropper
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/144-mastra-npm-packages-compromised-via.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:

logsource:

  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ip:
    DestinationIp:
      - '23.254.164.92'
      - '23.254.164.123'
  selection_dns:
    DestinationHostname:
      - 'hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com'
      - 'hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com'
  condition: selection_ip or selection_dns
level: critical
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationIp:(23.254.164.92 OR 23.254.164.123) OR @DestinationHostname:(hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com OR hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com))) OR (source:windows.defender @RemoteUrl:(*hwsrv-1327786* OR *hwsrv-1327785* OR */update/49890878*))
(#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemoteAddressIP4="23.254.164.92" OR RemoteAddressIP4="23.254.164.123")) OR (#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/hwsrv-132778[56]\.hostwindsdns\.com/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.app) as app sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes_out sum(All_Traffic.bytes_in) as bytes_in from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")) (All_Traffic.dest_port IN (8000,443)) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.app) as app sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes_out sum(All_Traffic.bytes_in) as bytes_in from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")) (All_Traffic.dest_port IN (8000,443)) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Node spawning detached script from %TEMP% with 24-hex filename and host:port argv (stage-2) AIInstallation High
Hunts the stage-2 execution shape unique to this dropper: node.exe launching a script whose basename matches ^[a-f0-9]{24}\.js$ located in the OS temp directory, with the stage-2 C2 host:port (e.g. 23.254.164.123:443) passed as the second argv. This combination is artifact-driven and has no legitimate analog. Rationale: The 24-hex-char .js filename in tmpdir and host:port argv pattern come directly from the kill-chain reconstruction's quoted spawn signature: child_process.spawn(process.execPath, [filepath, stage2C2], {cwd: os.tmpdir(), detached: true}). Both the filename shape and the trailing host:port argv are highly specific.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1564.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • npm pack/install creating randomly-named cache files that happen to match the 24-hex pattern (rare — npm uses longer hashes)
  • Internal build tools generating obfuscated cache files in TEMP
  • Electron app updaters writing temp staging scripts (typically named app-update.js etc., not bare hex)
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the Stage2Target column — if it resolves to 23.254.164.0/24 or hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com, treat as confirmed Mastra C2 callback. Capture the .js file from %TEMP% before it self-deletes. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached node process tree, preserve %TEMP% contents for forensics, block stage-2 IP/domain at perimeter. 3) Hunt: enumerate every secret on the host (env vars, ~/.aws, ~/.npmrc, ~/.config/gh, GitHub Actions runner secrets), assume compromised, rotate. Pivot on the package.json that pulled in easy-day-js to identify other infected hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(?:\\Temp\\|AppData\\Local\\Temp\\|/tmp/)[a-f0-9]{24}\.js\s+\S+:\d{2,5}"
| extend Stage2Target = extract(@"([a-zA-Z0-9\.\-]+:\d{2,5})\s*$", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, Stage2Target, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/node"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(?:\\Temp\\|AppData\\Local\\Temp\\|/tmp/)[a-f0-9]{24}\.js\s+\S+:\d{2,5}"
| extend Stage2Target = extract(@"([a-zA-Z0-9\.\-]+:\d{2,5})\s*$", 1, CommandLine)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, Stage2Target, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE) @CommandLine:(*\\Temp\\* OR *AppData\\Local\\Temp* OR */tmp/*) @CommandLine:(*23.254.164.123* OR *.js\ *:443* OR *.js\ *:8000*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(\\\\Temp\\\\|AppData\\\\Local\\\\Temp\\\\|/tmp/)[a-f0-9]{24}\\.js\\s+\\S+:\\d{2,5}", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent values(Processes.process_hash) as hash from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=node.exe OR Processes.process_name=node) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="(?i)(?:[\\\/]Temp[\\\/]|AppData[\\\/]Local[\\\/]Temp[\\\/]|\/tmp\/)[a-f0-9]{24}\.js\s+\S+:\d{2,5}" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent values(Processes.process_hash) as hash from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=node.exe OR Processes.process_name=node) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="(?i)(?:[\\\/]Temp[\\\/]|AppData[\\\/]Local[\\\/]Temp[\\\/]|\/tmp\/)[a-f0-9]{24}\.js\s+\S+:\d{2,5}" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
npm install referencing compromised @mastra packages or easy-day-js dependency AIDelivery High
Hunts hosts and CI runners executing npm/yarn/pnpm install that explicitly name easy-day-js or one of the 13 compromised @mastra package versions. Catches both intentional installs and those triggered by lockfile updates that resolved during the 36-minute attack window on 2026-06-17. Rationale: The full list of 13 compromised @mastra packages plus the easy-day-js typosquat dependency name come directly from the article's affected-versions table. Any command-line reference is article-specific by definition — this name was registered as a typosquat purely for this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra/issues/18045
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1199
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-aware developers running `npm view easy-day-js` to inspect the IOC
  • Incident-response forensic captures of infected lockfiles being read on analyst workstations
  • Mastra framework users who legitimately depend on @mastra/core but pinned to versions BEFORE 1.42.1 (the malicious release)
  • SCA tooling like socket.dev or snyk scanning package metadata
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("npm view","npm info","npm search","socket.dev","snyk","--dry-run")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host's package-lock.json/yarn.lock actually RESOLVED easy-day-js@1.11.22 (cmdline can name a package without installing the malicious version if pinned). Check resolved version, not declared range. 2) Contain: if the malicious version is resolved, isolate, rotate every secret accessible from that host (LLM keys, AWS, GitHub, NPM), purge node_modules and lockfile, force-pin @mastra packages to known-good versions. 3) Hunt: query CI/CD systems for any pipeline run between 2026-06-17 01:01 UTC and present that did `npm install` for any of the 13 affected packages — those builds installed the malicious dependency and any secrets in the runner environment must be considered burned.
let compromised = dynamic(["easy-day-js","@mastra/schema-compat","@mastra/core","@mastra/memory","@mastra/server","@mastra/deployer","@mastra/pg","@mastra/mcp","@mastra/libsql","@mastra/evals","@mastra/datadog","@mastra/rag","@mastra/deployer-vercel","@mastra/redis"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (compromised) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (compromised)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let compromised = dynamic(["easy-day-js","@mastra/schema-compat","@mastra/core","@mastra/memory","@mastra/server","@mastra/deployer","@mastra/pg","@mastra/mcp","@mastra/libsql","@mastra/evals","@mastra/datadog","@mastra/rag","@mastra/deployer-vercel","@mastra/redis"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any (compromised)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra dropper beacon file .pkg_history/.pkg_logs created by node in temp directory AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the campaign's victim-fingerprint files (.pkg_history, .pkg_logs) written to the OS temp directory by a node.exe process. These filenames are unique to the easy-day-js dropper and are used to record install path and compromised package name. Rationale: The .pkg_history and .pkg_logs file names in temp are explicit IOCs from the kill-chain reconstruction's quoted detection hint: 'Beacon: record install path and package name in tmp dir'. These dotfile names with that path constraint and node.exe writer have no benign analog.
ATT&CKT1083 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom internal npm tooling that happens to write a similarly-named beacon file
  • Other npm packages legitimately using .pkg_history (none known)
  • Forensic capture replay during IR exercises
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the contents of the .pkg_history / .pkg_logs file to confirm it lists @mastra package paths and easy-day-js. Capture the file before the dropper self-cleans. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node child, block 23.254.164.0/24 at egress, preserve %TEMP% for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessAccountName + DeviceId — query the previous 30 days of DeviceProcessEvents for the postinstall hook (UC1) and DeviceNetworkEvents for the C2 IPs (UC2) to scope the dwell time. Treat any secret accessible from this host as burned and rotate.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", "/tmp/", @"AppData\Local\Temp")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Temp\", "/tmp/", @"AppData\Local\Temp")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mastra Dropper Beacon File .pkg_history/.pkg_logs in Temp
id: 4a2b8c1d-9e3f-4b5a-87d2-1f6a3c4e9b21
description: Detects the easy-day-js dropper writing its victim-fingerprint files (.pkg_history / .pkg_logs) into the OS temp directory
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\Temp\\.pkg_history OR *\\Temp\\.pkg_logs OR *AppData\\Local\\Temp\\.pkg_history OR *AppData\\Local\\Temp\\.pkg_logs OR */tmp/.pkg_history OR */tmp/.pkg_logs) @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i TargetFileName=/(\\Temp\\|AppData\\Local\\Temp\\|\/tmp\/)\.(pkg_history|pkg_logs)$/i

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc values(Filesystem.file_path) as path from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")) Filesystem.action=created by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search path="*\\Temp\\*" OR path="*/tmp/*" OR path="*AppData\\Local\\Temp*" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

node.exe reading developer credential files shortly after npm install (Mastra stage-2) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the stage-2 credential harvest behaviour: a node.exe process reading ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml, or the GitHub Actions runner secrets directory shortly after an npm install. Aligns with the article's assessment that the dropper steals LLM/cloud/VCS tokens for exfil to 23.254.164.123:443. Rationale: Credential file paths (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.config/gh, GitHub Actions runner _temp dir, .npmrc) are from the kill-chain reconstruction's phase 8 quoted hint. The 10-minute join after npm install scopes to the dropper's actual execution window, cutting false positives from cloud-CLI tooling that legitimately reads these files at other times.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.005 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • aws-cli wrappers shelling out to node and immediately reading ~/.aws/credentials
  • Vercel/Netlify deploy CLI authenticated via gh token reading hosts.yml during build
  • Internal CI bootstrappers that read .npmrc as a normal part of npm install (would need refinement to filter)
  • Electron-based dev tools indexing user dotfiles for autocomplete
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("aws-sdk","@aws-sdk","vercel","netlify","firebase-tools")
Response runbook
1) Triage: cross-reference DeviceName + AccountName against UC4 hits (compromised @mastra install) and UC2 hits (C2 callback). Three-way correlation = high-confidence credential theft. 2) Contain: force-rotate every cred read by node — AWS keys in ~/.aws, GitHub PAT in ~/.config/gh, NPM publish tokens in ~/.npmrc, SSH keys. For CI runners, revoke runner registration tokens and re-provision. 3) Hunt: pivot the stolen credentials to CloudTrail/AzureActivity/GitHub audit log — search for the rotated AWS access key's last-used location, any unfamiliar IPs on the GitHub token usage, and any new npm publish events under the developer's account in the 24h post-infection window.
let CredentialReads = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where (FolderPath has @"\.aws\" and FileName == "credentials")
    or (FolderPath has "/.aws/" and FileName == "credentials")
    or (FolderPath has @"\.config\gh\" and FileName == "hosts.yml")
    or (FolderPath has "/.config/gh/" and FileName == "hosts.yml")
    or (FolderPath has @"\.ssh\" and FileName matches regex @"^id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)$")
    or (FolderPath has "Runner.Worker" and FolderPath has "_temp")
    or FileName =~ ".npmrc";
let RecentNpmInstall = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "npm" and ProcessCommandLine has "install"
| project NpmTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, NpmUser = AccountName;
CredentialReads
| join kind=inner RecentNpmInstall on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (NpmTime .. NpmTime + 10m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, NpmTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, NpmTime), InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let CredReads = ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where (TargetFilePath has @"\.aws\" and TargetFileName == "credentials")
    or (TargetFilePath has "/.aws/" and TargetFileName == "credentials")
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\.config\gh\" and TargetFileName == "hosts.yml")
    or (TargetFilePath has "/.config/gh/" and TargetFileName == "hosts.yml")
    or TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc"
    or (TargetFilePath has "Runner.Worker" and TargetFilePath has "_temp");
let NpmRuns = ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "npm" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "install"
| project NpmTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, NpmUser = ActorUsername;
CredReads
| join kind=inner NpmRuns on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (NpmTime .. NpmTime + 10m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, NpmTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, NpmTime), ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE) @TargetFilename:(*\\.aws\\credentials OR */.aws/credentials OR *\\.config\\gh\\hosts.yml OR */.config/gh/hosts.yml OR *\\.ssh\\id_rsa OR */.ssh/id_rsa OR *Runner.Worker*_temp*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i
| regex("(\\\\\\.aws\\\\credentials|/\\.aws/credentials|\\\\\\.config\\\\gh\\\\hosts\\.yml|/\\.config/gh/hosts\\.yml|\\\\\\.ssh\\\\id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|Runner\\.Worker.*_temp)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
